blocks.x: Questions to start off and then I'll...
We might get your name and your, the date of your birth. It would be nice to have them, just where you were born.
Yes, and where you were born.
Yes, those things too.
Well, I usually forget.
A little bit about your life too. We would be interested in knowing naturally too about your life and early albums when you were a girl. So if it's running okay, if you want. It's running okay.

Well, I'm Stella Oliver, the widow of King Joe Oliver. We have been married, we married in 1912, July the 13th. Was a fine man, a fine husband, and a fine musician. We got along beautifully together. We traveled around, had our ups and downs together, but we still stuck. And I'm happy to say this morning that I'm, I'm glad to say a few words about Joe. He's dead now, nearly 18 years. He died 38. And I miss him quite a night. I miss him up until now. However, his name has lived in the public. He was a great musician and a great man. Everybody loved him. And I still love him too. Now, Joe was, I was born in Donisonville. A little place above, Abin where Joe was born. He was born in Abin. He's this brother, he has three sisters, no brother.
Or any of the brothers, or any of the other sisters, anyone else in the family living? Yes.
He has one sister in Arizona, and he has one in New York, and I think the one in Chicago died. I don't hear from him regularly now.
But the one in New York is still living?
Is still living, yes. Is that Mrs. Johnson? Mrs. Johnson, that's Mrs. Johnson, who he loved dearly. We lived with her about three years in New York.

Oh, excuse me for interrupting. Is that chair comfortable? I put the microphone on this side. Would you rather... Mrs. No, this is chair comfortable. Because I thought maybe you wanted to lean against the back more. Mrs. No, this is... Yes. Is that all right? Because we could put the microphone on the other side. Mrs. And then...
Excuse me if I'm interrupting. Mrs. That's all right. Well, if I'm not just right...
No, that's fine. I thought it wouldn't make it comfortable for you, though.
Mrs. Joe was born in Abin.
Is that on the other side of the river, or this side?
Mrs. That's on the other side. The other side.
Yes.

Mrs. Near Donaldsonville. Near Donaldsonville, just three miles from where I was born. But I didn't know him as children. We didn't come in contact with each other. But his mother worked at a place called Salzburg. That was a plantation. But Joe was born in Abin. And when he came to New Orleans as a boy...
Excuse me, do you remember just when he was born, his birth date? Yes. He was born in...
On December the 19th. Nineteen... Nineteen... Nineteen... Eighteen... Eighteen... Eighteen... Eighteen... Eighteen... Eighteen...
Eighty-five.

Eighty-five. Eighty-five. Eighty-five. Eighty-five. I'm just a few years younger than Joe. And we met when we was in New Orleans working. We met... He was working two doors from me, where I work. And he was working for some Jewish family. They raised him. He was there as a boy. He didn't know much about Conrad, but he was determined to learn. So he started rehearsing, practicing, and he did fairly well.
Do you know when he moved to the city? Did he tell you when he moved?
No, I don't know. I only know him after he came to New Orleans. And we were two doors from each other on Magazine Street working.
Was that the place near Second Street? Yeah, Magazine and Second.
I was on Second and he was on Magazine... He was on Magazine near Second.
Near Second.
Yes. And when I met him, he was quite a young man. We were both going along in the courtenayes, running around together and all.
How long did you know him before he was married about?
Before we married? Oh, well, I knew him about four or five years before we were married.
So he was in the city several years before 1912.

Oh, yes. We married in 1912. We married in 1912. He was in the city quite a long time. His mother had passed and as a boy he went there and he lived on premises. And they probably just took him like their own family. They raised him. He did like he wanted and he started rehearsing for music. Well, he went off on a little tour up above Donisonville and he was stranded as a boy. The man took a couple of boys. Did he play in coronet then? He was playing the coronet then. And then he got stranded. He didn't have anything. But he played too loud. The man took him off of, he was playing then first trambone. He started on the trambone. Yes, but he played too loud for the trambone and then they put him on the coronet. And then that's the time I met Joe. And after I met Joe, of course we went around a long time together. And he got to going around playing at different dances. And he used to play at these balls. He'd have balls and he'd play. And of course then he got so good he didn't want to work anymore. And we met and we married.
What kind of work had he been doing on that?

He had been doing just ordinary work. Yard boy, they used to call him then. They'd clean the yard around him. And he could get off any time he wanted. And he got off any time he wanted. And they were very good to him. Didn't pay much of a salary, but they raised him. They raised him.
His mother died when he was quite young then? Oh, before I met him.
I had never met his mother.
Did he ever say anything about his father? No, but his... Did he play any instrument or anything?

No, his father didn't. His father, he always told me his father was a minister. He was a minister? Yes. His mother was named Virginia. And his father was named Henry. But I didn't meet him until his mother had passed. That's when he was in New Orleans. And after I met him, and he began playing. And then we got quite chummy. And he began to get popular. They used to play on the trucks.
Oh, yes. I've heard about them.

Yes. And they used to play... If they were going to have a dance, they'd advertise that dance. They'd get on a corner and they'd play, and Joe would play at the top of his voice. And he could hear him for three or four blocks and we'd blow him that horn. Then he had me to fire him around with eggs. Hard-boiled eggs. That always gave him... He said a lot of... In other words, it made him strong. Give him more strength and play. Yes. The hard-boiled eggs.
Did he have a sandwich for him? No, just the eggs.
Just the hard-boiled plain eggs. I'm busy in the kitchen.
Uh-huh.

And he would take these eggs and he'd go on blowing. They'd get out of the corner and the people would gang around them. Sometimes on Sunday, there were two bands. They'd meet on this corner. And one would try to play the other. Play out the other. That was Celestine. That passed recently. Yes. And all the other bunch.
And it was like a Mardi Gras day. Everybody was out to hear the band.

And Joe was blowing. And after that, he began playing just dances. And he began playing up at Tulane. He organized the band. Did he have his own band? Or had he played with another band, do you know? No, he hadn't played with another band. They would just get musicians here and there. You see, all over New Orleans, they had quite a few musicians. Not like now. He knew all of them and then hardly had a job, standard job. But he would get them up, gather them up and they'd say, we play on Sunday evening. And they would have this truck and they'd go from corner to corner all over town. And they'd say, we played Sunday evening. And they'd have this truck and they'd go from corner to corner all over town. And then after that, Joe organized a band. The first band he played with was a brass band. It was Onward. Onward.
Yes. And the Magnolia. Well, they used to play parades. The Magnolia and Onward both?

Yes. He played with both bands. And they would play street parades like the organization would turn out. And they'd walk for blocks and blocks and blocks just playing music. Well, then after that, as far as I can remember, Joe had a couple of little bands down in the district. He worked down there. They'd get a dollar a night. And we lived beautifully on that dollar a night. During that time.
Did they get tips much in the district? Oh, yes. Oh, yes.

Oh, yes. They got tips. And the tips was all made, put in a box. Yes. And it was each out of one to the other. Every man would get so much. Whenever they got, every man would get it. But then he played down there for a long, long time. And after he played down there, he had a little band playing at a stable, they call it, on Padre Street. Used to play around there. Well... At a stable? It was a dance hall. That they fixed up for the... For the... To dance. To dance, yes. To dance. And they raided them one night. Took Joe to the... Took Joe's band and everybody was in there. But Joe thought it was terrible. He said a man working for... Making an honest living to the raided man, take him to jail. And that's why he left New Orleans. He never came back. Then he went to Chicago. There was a lady running a dance hall on 35th Street. Thirty... Thirty-first. Thirty-first. Oh, yes. Thirty-first. That was the Royal... The Royal Garden played for Miss Major. A lady named Miss Major. And he went there and he played. He was quite a success there. So... He got a big job to play at the plantation. That was black and tan. It made it quite a success there. A beautiful review and everything there. But after a while and the probation come in... Everything... The beginning of the radio all around... Joe was out of work. But in the meantime... Joe got Louis... To have Miss Major. With him. With him. Louis promised him when he left you that he would come. If he got a good job. Yeah. He got a good job. Well, Louis was young then. He was very young. He used to run errand first. He'd come to my house then. But a boy... He'd come to my house and make errand first. And he followed Joe. Every step Joe went around. And Joe was fond of him. He was fond of Joe. And I used to always call him my boy. Mm-hm. Well... Louis got a job. Kendall and Joe got a job. So they went to St. Louis on the boat. The steamer...
Sidney I believe what their name was. Yes. It was one of the boats. I think the St. Paul sometime around there. Yes. Sidney though I believe was the main one they worked on first.
After he worked on this boat... Joe went to Chicago. He got this job. at this job. It was a fairly nice job it was made.
Do you remember his very first job? Was it the Royal Garden or do you remember the Dreamland?

Was he there? Oh that was in Chicago. In Chicago, I thought I meant. And then he worked at the Pekin. That was after hours for all the actress and actress. They worked at 6 o'clock in the morning. After everything was over, all the actress and actresses, big name, would come to the Pekins.
How did he get the first job in Chicago? Did he go up and look around or did somebody

send for him? No, Miss Major sent for him. Sent for him. He got the job for him. She sent for him and he had in his band, he carried for me, Jonathan Sear, a banjo player. Jimmy Noon, a clarinet player. And the two Dodge brothers, they left here with him to go to Chicago to play his first job in Chicago.
And, uh, what's the other one? It was the trombone. Nora Dutrie. Nora Dutrie. I know he made some records with him.

Yes. And, um, well they had quite a nice band up there. They went over there. It was a great band. Yes, it was. Because all the, uh, all the downtown big folks used to come to the Dreamland, to the Royal Garden to hear Joe play. Him and Louie then were playing together. Mm-hmm. And they used to make what they called then bricks. Yes. When Louie would make a brick, Joe would catch it just like that. And it was the prettiest thing. I wished I had some records.
I have those records. I've heard them. They're beautiful. Beautiful music.

Well, they worked a long time together and things began to get bad again. Then Louie went over to the, what's the name of this, theater on, uh, State Street. State near 35th. Oh, the Vandome was that? Uh-huh. And then Dome. Louie went then over to play there. They sort of split. Joe didn't have much work and we went over there and he played. He played for a long time with, uh, I think it must have been, with, uh, Tate. Oh, yes. Yes, I knew him. Erskine Tate. Erskine Tate, right. And they played and it was quite a success for a long time. Then all the time Joe was playing this, little hole in the wall, I call them, like the Pecan and Miss Major. And of course it kept him quite busy. Then he got this big job, plantation. That was a big job. It was black and tan. It was on, on South Park and 35th. And with Peyton. Peyton had a review there. Dave Peyton. I met him once in Chicago. Joe played with him, but he didn't care so much for, Joe didn't care so much for him. So from there, after that was closed down, that's the time Joe went to New York. But he made quite a success around Chicago. Yes, I knew him. Playing at the Dreamland with all the actors and playing at the Peking. And he made quite a success. He made a name for himself. That's where he began to go over. Began to be in here. And he made Dipper Mouth Blues. Yes. That's Joe's own number. That's our own number. He composed that. But he told me that was the first piece he ever made. And he sold it outright. He sold it. How about that? That's too bad. Just for a few pennies. He said he didn't know any different. Well, I don't know. It went from that bad to worse after he went to New York. Because nobody sent for him in New York. He just went there on a wild goose chase just for two or three nights for a week staying. Well, it wasn't a success. His band wasn't a success. Or was with him then. And Blue Trey. And Red Alum. Red Alum. And Nicholson. Nickson. Albin Nicholos. Yes.
Clarenette. Clarenette. Clarenette. Yes.

Is that Paul Barbrun? Do you remember? Paul Barbrun. Paul Barbrun also. He was playing on drums then. Yes. And they played around New York for a long time. They did fairly well but not much because men began to get tired and Ory was there too. He began to spit. He began to leave Joe. Because he wasn't so strong anymore and all that traveling around and disappointment and all. And Joe was quite disappointed.
I heard once that Joe had some trouble with his teeth about that time. Is that true?

I'm coming along to that time. Then his teeth was getting bad. He was in New York. Then he thought he'd take the roll. Here and there. A little nightstand. And of course all the time the teeth was giving him trouble. And he was failing on the coronet. Was he losing his teeth or just? Piree of the gums. Piree. Piree of the gums. And he went to Nashville, Tennessee on a little job. Well then that's where he made his mistake. He began to go down. His teeth began to get bad and all. And he played for a long time around Nashville. But nothing to it. Nothing to it. You see? The contracts called for so many men being on the job, setting such an hour. And if he wasn't there, the band was so highly responsible. Because Joe had all the fellas got along together. But they wasn't up to par. They didn't realize what they were going to lose. And they did lose the band. And Joe stayed in Nashville quite a while. I went over there. But there was nothing to that.
That was the depression too. Those years. Yes it was. Very, very hard. Very, very hard. We did have a little money. We lost it all at Chicago Bank.

Then there was nothing. He couldn't get nothing. And then they went, as I say, Red Bank, New York, played around in there. And almost all the men was getting tired. Getting disgusted. So they broke up. Or we went to California. John Cincere came back here. Dutrie, I think he went to California too. But he passed. Yes, he didn't live long. He didn't live long at all. Because he was gassed in the Army. That's what I heard. Yes. And that caused his death, you see. He was a fine musician. And then we went. It comes in time that we went to San Francisco. The band went to San Francisco. Oh yes. Did you go with them all that year? Yes, I went. And Lil Armstrong. That's where Lil met Louis. Lil Armstrong and Louis. That's where they was married. He met her in Los Angeles because Joe had taken the whole band out there. But they played at a five to ten cents dance. They didn't do nothing. It was just a white goose chase everywhere they went. They didn't do anything.
Well that was the one on Market Street in San Francisco. Oh, on Market Street. That's right. I took a picture of that place. It's still there. It's still there, yes. It's a pool hall now, isn't it?
I went there with them. And Lily also, she went and she and Louis made it and of course they remember.

Do you remember, somebody told me that another lady, whom I know, I think she's dead now, Bertha Gonsolin played piano with the band. Do you remember? Bertha Gonsolin. Bertha Gonsolin. She came from here. Her father had been on the railroad, the SP. And somebody told me she played piano part of the time out there. That Lil left or something and came back to Chicago. Do you remember her, Bertha Gonsolin? No, I don't remember Bertha. She probably wasn't with the band long.

Very long, no. She wasn't. Because after they stayed out there, one by one, they each left. And Joe went down, as I said, and his teeth was very bad. He had teeth put in but they were never successful.
He tried false teeth. Oh, he did, yes. I never knew that.

And then he tried a new system. He was telling me about it. That instead of blowing with the pressure, putting it to your lip for the pressure, he blowed from the tongue and the teeth. Oh, yeah. Yes. And he did fine. But of course, all the time he was going to be an old man. And he had so much disappointment all the time he was going back, you see. But he blew very well at a number of years like that.
It's real easy without any pressure.

Yes. That's right. Without any pressure. So after that we came back, we went back to Chicago from California. We went back to Chicago. And then from Chicago, where did we go? Where did we go? Where did we go? In Chicago, where did we go? African. We went back to Chicago and then we went to New York. And that's where we made the free. I had it all backward. That's where he started around, I see.
Somebody told me once that he went to St. Louis for a trip, I think just a short trip. Do you remember going there? Oh, yes. Yes. No, I didn't go with him.

You didn't go on those trips? Yeah. All the time Joe would take a trip like that. He went to St. Louis. He went to St. Louis. That's the time he brought Louis. He went to try to coax Louis to leave the boat. That's the time. And he made the short trip. I have a picture of you. Of Louis and Joe. And they stayed there quite a long time. But Joe liked sports. He would go to New York for the ball game. Well, somebody told me he liked the ball game. Oh, yes. He liked all the sports. He was crazy about ball game. And ball game and pool. I used to bring his dinner to the Dreamland. He liked the pool so well he wouldn't come home for dinner. He would call me up and tell me, bring his dinner over to the Dreamland. But he never ate anywhere but home. He wasn't a fella to eat sandwiches and all that. He wanted salad food all that time. Somebody told me he was a big eater. He was. He really did eat a lot. He was a big eater. And he liked good things and he liked nice things. He was crazy about sweets. And he didn't mind spending his money for it and for his friends. He was very liberal with his money with his friends. Because I've gone through his bank book and find out where he had sent money here to Palau. Palau. Oh, yes. The violin player. That's right. That's right. His whole family was sick. Joe would send money out of his salad. He would do that. And he wouldn't tell me anything until I'd look and see. Yeah. He'd send it. But it seemed so bad. The fellas didn't stick with him. Yeah, that's a shame. They didn't. And they didn't say nice things. Some things they said about him. I read a couple of books. They didn't say nice things about him. And he had a wonderful disposition. Nice personality. He liked a kid when he was a good year.
That's what I heard him like. He was a big joker.

If you wasn't a kid out there, don't stop at Joe. Because he could kid you and he'd make you so mad. And he never got mad. But he just liked a kid. He liked a kid. And everything was good natured with him. He wasn't hardly serious with anything. But he loved his home. He did. He loved his home. He was a man that didn't stay out all night. Gallivanting around. Because Lily used to tell me all the time. Joe said, I got to go home to that chicken. He called me the chicken all the time. He says, I got to go home to that chicken. He never would stay out. He wasn't a drinking man. Fall from it.
Somebody told me about that. He used to like that sugar water. Just put sugar in water.

Yes. Sometimes when he'd go out to eat or he'd be caught on the road. He'd always eat the Chinaman food. He liked that. He liked that because he could go away and the sugar bowl was on the table. And then he would keep the sugar bowl right by him. And get a great big glass and water would never get out of that glass. He'd keep adding water and sugar until he had enough. It would be lemonade or anything just plain water. No, just plain sugar water. Plain sugar water.
Somebody told me they wondered maybe if he had diabetes or something when he used all that sugar. Do you think that he had any trouble at that time?

No, I don't think he had any trouble with it. I don't know. Because he never complained. Never. He seemed to be well then. He seemed to be well all the time. But after he began to get older, he was always depressed. He was always thinking, thinking, thinking all the time. Sometimes at night, he'd jump up out of the bed. And I'd ask him, what on earth happened to jump up out of the bed? He said, something came to me, music. And he'd get up and get that carnet. And he'd blow them notes, whatever they were. And the next morning he'd put them together. Well, I didn't understand what it was all about. Did he write them down then? Yes, he would write them down. He'd write them down before he'd go back to bed and go to sleep. But as I said, I think Joe could have lasted longer. Had he been a fella, the fella would stick to understand. He was very hard to understand. Once you met him, you'd like it. But he was hard to understand. When a man don't drink with everybody, they don't understand you. Especially those kind of men. They expect you to drink with them. Then you'd talk a little bit more than you would talk if you didn't drink. And he didn't drink. He was hard. I had so many of his friends that tell me that they can't understand him. But he was really a genius. Yes, he must have been. He was really a genius. But as I said, he didn't want anybody to go ahead of a band, like to sell your band. He wanted to do all that himself. And he had no regular income. You know, if you take a band out on the road, or they sell your band, you've got to have money. He went to most every big place. He was losing money all the time. Because sometimes the fellas, he would get a big job after he got on the road. He'd get a big job. And they would demand the band to be at 7 o'clock. If it rained, if it doesn't rain before 7. If it rained, then the contract was broken. Now, some of the men was out gallivanting, drinking. He didn't know where to find them. He told me a lot of time he had to pick and pick the instrument out of pawn and all of that. He went through all of that. Well, it was hard on him. It was hard. And his last years was...
It must have been very bad, huh? Very bad. I heard he had a bus too and had trouble with that bus and all too.

He bought a bus in Nashville, Tennessee. And once he bought a... What do you call this? Truck? Truck actually. Mail truck. Oh, yeah. Mail truck. But that was to carry the band, the music and the instrument and all the music. And they wouldn't let him use that out there in Nashville, Tennessee. Well, they wouldn't let him use the mail truck. No, no. They wouldn't let him use that. He bought that to travel around. Yes. Go to little short places, you know. But, as I said, he was a happy-go-lucky sort of a fellow, in a way. He was like of a dial disposition because... And he'd do anything for you. Anything. Nothing was too much trouble. And his money wasn't too good to spend. But, I don't know, for some reason, I always say that the fellows didn't stick enough with Joe. I don't know why, but they were... Maybe he would have been living now, had he gone to somebody and tell him. And they could have given him an understanding how to do and how to get along. But he didn't. He kept it all to himself. And the last days, he wasn't so sick. He wasn't so sick. For a grand man. And like I said, just... If he'd have just lived five more years, he wouldn't realize what he was.
He'd have been popular again. Oh, yes. People would have appreciated him then again. They do now, but it's too late. Yes, yes. It's too late. It's too late. Yes, it's too late.
But, as I said, he was a grandfella to know. Grandfella to know. But he wanted to manage his own business.
Well, it would be better that way if he could have made it that way, rather than the manager takes half of their pay sometimes, too, you know.

That's what he said. But you can't make it all. No, that's right. No. Look, Louie and Louie wouldn't be in Louie Armstrong today. Yes, that's right. As if he didn't have the manager, somebody behind him. And sometimes even the men go ahead of him. Yes. See what treatment they get. Because they get an awful hard treatment. Musicians, some people don't want them in their house. Yes, that's right. And their meals, sometimes they don't have the meals and all of that. But as I can remember, so many things. And when Louie was in St. Louis, he'd come home and stop with us. And he just loved you. He idolized you. He idolized you. And Joe was crazy about him. They'd come home and I'd fix red beans for them. I know they like red beans. Well, whenever Louie would go home, I had red beans. And I'd cook a big pot and put it in a big dish and put it on the table. And we used to put the hot bones, what they call them. That was the best meat. It's near the knee bone, you know. Oh, yes. And you cook that until it's done, red beans. And you put it in the beans. That's ham, is it? Ham, yes. Ham, yes. And season up them beans and he and Louie would wash that bone. They'd wash it. Louie would wash it. Joe would wash Louie. And all of a sudden they'd make a great big jump to make us laugh. They'd have fun. They'd see who was going to get that last bone. But they were funny. To be together, they had a lot of fun together. Those two boys had a lot of fun together. And he'd come home and he'd stop. Well, when he'd stop home with me, he'd give, after Louie would come back from playing, he'd get his dress. He'd give all of us a physique. Everybody got to take physique with Louie. Everybody got to take physique.
Louie's still there, right? He's still, he's a thriss-criss.

Yeah, that's right, that's right, that's right. I had a lot of fun with those two boys. I had a lot of fun with all of the boys. All of the boys. Every one of them. And I liked them all. But, as I say, Joe was only 54 when he died. He wasn't really old at all. No! He should've, I thought he should've at least lived until he was 65, 70. Yes, he should've lived. Because a man that doesn't drink, and it didn't dissipate as I say. He didn't dissipate.
Was he always pretty heavy when he was a boy? Always, always. Sort of. Always.

Always. Because he always ate cornbread and he had salad food and very few things he didn't like. And he drank plenty of water. Plenty of water. Plenty of water all the time. He had water kept him fat.
Yes, because of the starches, I guess. Yes. Lee Collins told me too, when he went to Chicago, you had a big meal for him the first night you got there.

Oh, yes. Oh, yes. I always, I was always nice with the boys. Because I wanted to always remember me as Joe's wife. And Joe was so nice to me. He was so nice to me. So good to me and my people. So I had to try to make him happy. And the only way to do it was to treat his friends nice.
Sure.

That was the only way I know. I couldn't repay him in any other way. I had to be nice. And all I could do was just cook a big pot of beans and tell them all come over. And that's all they wanted. Beans and rice. And Lee Collins and Dutre and Ori and the whole gang of mine have them sometimes. And Joe liked company too. He liked company. He was very fond of company. And he liked for them to eat. But as I said, he wasn't a drinking man. He wasn't a drinking man at all. But he had, he had a hard time with it. He had a bad time.
Where did you live in Chicago? Do you remember which street it was about?

Yes. I lived on Prairie, near 31st. The first place I lived when we went to Chicago, we lived right on 39th Street, 39th and Vernon. That was it. Then Mr. Glazer had a place that I didn't know him then. But he had some kind of a place back there, a dance or something, a dance hall or something. I didn't go around that much to the place in Chicago because I was kind of strange, you know. But he had some, that's where Joe met him.
Later he had the sunset. I don't know what he had first before that. Well, it was a small place then. Small place too.
I think, I am not sure, so I won't say that. I thought he had the, I thought he had the plantation. But that, no, that plantation was a small place.

Later he, Joe had the place across the street where Louie played at the sunset and the plantation. I don't know. dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear
I was wondering about up at Donaldsonville, the very first music you can remember when

you were a girl. Do you remember any of the, did they have any parades or dance bands, what kind of bands in the country and all around there too? Well, we didn't have much of a band. The band used to come from New Orleans. Mostly the bands from here.
And they didn't give, that's a small town, Donaldsonville. Yes. And a girl couldn't go to a dance. Couldn't go to a dance.
No, not like a boy who runs all over town.

You had to have the meditation. You wasn't allowed to dance. So the girls didn't get around much. And they had no band there. Whenever they were going to have a band, they'd send to New Orleans and a band would come down. But they didn't have all of this gallivanting around and going on because it was very straight town, little town, beautiful town, beautiful. And they were nice people, nice people to know. And the streets was all, old flowers all over the streets and everything.
Do you remember any parades? Did they have any brass bands on the streets? Any parades when you were a girl?
In Donaldsonville? No. No, we didn't have that.
I wondered about the music and the churches too.
Oh yes, yes. We had churches and all of my family belonged to church. And they used to have baptizing.
Is that a Baptist church?
That's a Baptist church. But my family is Creole. So we mixed up. Some are Baptist and some are Catholic.
You know what, did Joe belong to any church? Do you remember?
He never did belong to any church, but his mother was Baptist.
His father was probably a Baptist preacher.

Yes, that's right. That's right. And Joe is always crazy about the hymns. And he used to kid me and laugh. He'd take some of the hymns and make some songs with it. But finally, they did, eventually they did because when the saints were marching in, that was a hymn.
All those numbers, I close your walk and glory land, they used by and by.
That's right.

segments.title: Opening: name, birth and background questions
segments.summary: The interviewer sets up the recording and asks Stella Oliver for her name, birth details and early life.

segments.title: Widow of King Oliver; Joe's family and birthplace Abbeville
segments.summary: Stella introduces herself as Joe Oliver's widow, married 1912, and talks about both being born near Donaldsonville and his surviving sisters, including Mrs. Johnson in New York. A microphone and chair interruption occurs.

segments.title: Meeting Joe on Magazine Street and his boyhood
segments.summary: She met Joe in New Orleans, where he worked as a yard boy for a family that raised him, took up cornet after trombone, and courted her for four or five years before 1912. His parents were Virginia and Henry, a minister.

segments.title: Truck bands, brass bands and the district in New Orleans
segments.summary: Joe played on advertising trucks, with hard-boiled eggs for strength, in band contests, with the Onward and Magnolia brass bands, and in district bands at a dollar a night with shared tips.

segments.title: Raid on the Padre Street stable and leaving for Chicago
segments.summary: After Joe's band was raided at a dance hall, he left New Orleans for Chicago, the Royal Garden, the Plantation, and then the riverboat trip with Louis.

segments.title: First Chicago job and the Dreamland band with Louis
segments.summary: Miss Major sent for Joe, who took Johnny St. Cyr, Jimmy Noone and the Dodds brothers, with Dutrey, to Chicago. Joe and Louis played together at the Dreamland and Royal Garden.

segments.title: Erskine Tate, Plantation, Dave Peyton and Dipper Mouth Blues
segments.summary: Louis moved to the Vendome while Joe played with Erskine Tate and at small spots, then the Plantation with Dave Peyton. Joe sold Dipper Mouth Blues outright before going to New York.

segments.title: Failed New York trip, teeth trouble and Nashville
segments.summary: Joe went to New York with no job waiting; the band did poorly and Ory and others left. Gum disease damaged his playing and he worked in Nashville under contract troubles, during the Depression.

segments.title: California trip, Lil and Louis, and Joe's new embouchure
segments.summary: The band went to San Francisco and Los Angeles for poor dances, Lil Armstrong met Louis, men left one by one, and Joe tried false teeth and blowing from tongue and teeth before they returned to Chicago and New York.

segments.title: Joe's St. Louis trip, sports, appetite and generosity
segments.summary: Joe went to St. Louis to coax Louis off the boat, loved ball games and pool, ate well and sent money to Palao's sick family. She dislikes the unkind things said of him in books.

segments.title: Home-loving, non-drinking Joe and the sugar water
segments.summary: Joe stayed home, did not drink, kidded people, and drank sugar water in restaurants. Stella doubts he was diabetic.

segments.title: Joe's late years: genius, band management and the bus
segments.summary: Joe wrote tunes at night, was hard to understand because he did not drink, managed his own band and lost money. He bought a bus in Nashville and a mail truck and died young.

segments.title: Managers, musicians' treatment and red beans with Louis
segments.summary: Stella discusses managers and hard treatment of musicians, then recalls cooking red beans for Joe and Louis Armstrong whenever Louis visited.

segments.title: Joe's health, build, and feeding the band
segments.summary: Joe died at 54, was heavy as a boy, and Stella fed bands such as Lee Collins, Dutrey and Ory with beans and rice.

segments.title: Where they lived in Chicago and Mr. Glaser's place
segments.summary: Stella recalls living near 31st Street and 39th and Vernon in Chicago, and the Glaser dance hall and Plantation. The last block is garbled repetition.

segments.title: Growing up in Donaldsonville: no bands, no dances for girls
segments.summary: Donaldsonville was a small straight town where bands came from New Orleans and girls were not allowed to dance.

segments.title: Church, hymns and funeral music
segments.summary: Her Creole family was Baptist and Catholic, Joe's mother was Baptist, Joe loved hymns, and bands played hymns at funerals.

segments.title: Comments on rock and roll bands
segments.summary: A brief fragment about rock and roll bands and a band heard on television.
